He also stated that his salary with the Falcons had ranged from $10 million to $12 million and admitted that he had not managed his finances responsibly.

Vick also intends to partner with the Humane Society of the United States on efforts to fight dogfighting, Humane Society President Wayne Pacelle told CNN on Tuesday. Vick, the former Atlanta Falcons quarterback, was released from the federal penitentiary in Leavenworth, Kansas, after serving most of a 23-month sentence for his role in a dogfighting conspiracy operated from a property he owned in rural Surry County, Virginia. He was expected to spend the final weeks of his sentence confined to his home in Hampton, monitored by federal authorities and subject to strict conditions.

His release marks the beginning of a complicated and uncertain public re-entry: Vick remains suspended from the NFL, is trying to emerge from bankruptcy, and is seeking to rebuild his reputation through a partnership with the Humane Society of the United States.

Vick’s case became one of the most notorious scandals in modern sports. Federal prosecutors said he helped finance and participate in an interstate dogfighting operation known as “Bad Newz Kennels,” where dogs were trained to fight and where underperforming animals were killed. Vick pleaded guilty in 2007, admitting that he helped bankroll the operation and was involved in the deaths of dogs.

The fallout was swift. The Falcons moved on without him, endorsement deals vanished, and NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell suspended him indefinitely. Once the league’s highest-paid player, Vick entered bankruptcy as he faced millions of dollars in debts.

Now, as he leaves prison, Vick is attempting to navigate several paths at once: satisfying the terms of his criminal sentence, gaining approval of a repayment plan in bankruptcy court, persuading the NFL he deserves another chance, and convincing a skeptical public that he has changed.

Under home confinement, Vick is expected to be permitted to work, subject to approval. Reports at the time of his release indicated he had lined up a construction-related job as part of his transition. Federal home confinement typically includes electronic monitoring, restrictions on travel and a requirement that the inmate remain at an approved residence except for work, legal obligations, medical needs or other authorized activities.

His criminal sentence is scheduled to be followed by a period of supervised release, during which he will remain under federal oversight.

Vick’s financial situation may be nearly as challenging as his legal one. He filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection while incarcerated, listing substantial debts to creditors that included banks, former agents, attorneys and the Falcons. Bankruptcy proceedings exposed the depth of his financial collapse after years of large NFL salaries and endorsement income.

Court filings showed Vick’s representatives attempting to craft a plan to repay creditors over time, a process that could depend heavily on whether he is allowed to return to professional football. Without NFL income, his ability to satisfy debts would be sharply limited.

That possibility now rests largely with Goodell, who has said Vick’s conduct must be evaluated before any reinstatement. The league has not committed to a timetable. Goodell previously indicated that Vick would need to demonstrate genuine remorse and an understanding of the seriousness of his actions before being considered for a return.

Before his conviction, he was one of the league’s most dynamic players, a rare quarterback whose speed and improvisational ability changed defensive game plans. But after nearly two years away from the sport, teams would have to weigh his conditioning, timing and ability to adapt, along with fan and sponsor reaction.

Vick’s attempt at rehabilitation includes a highly visible alliance with the Humane Society of the United States, an organization that was among the most prominent voices condemning dogfighting after his arrest. The partnership drew mixed reactions from animal advocates, some of whom argued that Vick should not be given a public platform so soon after prison. To others, the brutality of the crimes makes forgiveness difficult, especially given the details of how dogs were treated and killed.
